HP Sprocket Portable Color Photo Printer, Print Social Media Photos on 2x3" Sticky-Backed Paper - Black (X7N08A) This is a great improvement over an earlier-gen ZINK paper ("zero ink") portable printer we have, which requires a wired connection and a proprietary charger, and no longer holds a charge well.

The HP Sprocket connects and prints wirelessly, charges from a standard micro-USB cable, and has a lithium-ion battery which is sure to last a lot longer.

We had it unboxed and printing in less than 5 minutes. You run it from a free app available for Android or Apple iOS devices. We used the Android version and it works great.

It takes less than 30 seconds to wirelessly send and print a photo. The prints are 2 inches by 3 inches, smooth and glossy, good resolution, and have a peel-and-stick backing for quick and easy mounting. In the long run, the priciest thing about a ZINK printer is the paper, so shop around for deals.

The prints came out a little to the warm side in color when sent "as is," but the app allows a lot of enhancement and has lots of effects you can add.

The Sprocket printer itself measures only 3 inches by 5 inches and less than an inch thick, and weighs about 6-and-a-half ounces. It's very portable.

And it's loads of fun.
text_fidelity_b: HP Sprocket Portable Color Photo Printer, Print Social Media Photos on 2x3" Sticky-Backed Paper - Black (X7N08A)

text_fidelity_a:
Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black I've been testing this Epson ProSense watch for the past week. I also have a 2-year-old Garmin Vivoactive HR watch that has most of the same features, but costs half as much. To the compare the two, I've been wearing one watch on each wrist and going on runs and bike rides to see how their readings compare. Both watches have daily step counters that give similar results (today, Garmin says 12044 steps while Epson says 12790 steps). 5% difference is close enough for me.

When I use the GPS exercise mode, the results start showing big differences. On today's run, Garmin recorded 4.02 miles while Epson says 3.9 miles. That's a 3% difference which is close enough for me. Garmin says 529 calories and Epson says 955 calories. Garmin says 535 feet of elevation gain and Epson says 1142 feet. I know Garmin has a barometric altimeter, while Epson is using GPS elevation, which is notoriously inaccurate. Does Epson's terrible elevation data cause a wildly inaccurate calorie count? I could not find any information on Epson's calorie calculation in their documentation, so I really cannot trust it.

Both devices give me heart rate readings with graphs by time or broken out by training zones. The numbers look close enough for my purposes. Both devices also give me maps of my route, which is is nice to have for reviewing later, especially if it is a new route to me.

The Epson is a much larger device (both width and thickness), as shown in the photo. While the Garmin is not especially attractive, at least it is relatively unobtrusive. Epson is big enough to feel clunky on my wrist, especially if I am wearing it all day (to take advantage of the step counter).

Both devices have a smartphone app that syncs your data and also sends notifications to the watch. I'm using this watch with a Google Pixel Android phone. The Garmin app by default uploads your data to the Garmin website. With Epson, you have to upload to a 3rd party website like Strava, which may not be compatible with all the data that your device is collecting.

Notifications work much better with Garmin than Epson. For incoming phone calls, both Garmin and Epson will display the caller ID or contact name so I don't have to pull out my phone to see who is calling. For incoming emails, Garmin displays the sender name and subject line, while Epson just says "you have mail". For text messages, Garmin shows the contact name and message. Epson shows no notification for text messages.

The only advantage (for my use case) that I can find with this Epson watch is the much longer battery life. Garmin claims 1 week of battery life with the GPS off or 13 hours with the GPS on. Epson claims 46 hours of battery life with the GPS on, which I suppose is great for some ultra endurance sports. For me, I never exercise more than 8 hours in a day.
text_fidelity_b: Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black

Kodak PlayFull ZE2 Waterproof Video Camera with 2x Optical Zoom and 2-Inch LCD Screen (Black) Though I use Windows XP, my computer is old and my processor (Sempron) is not what is required to run the "KODAK Share Button" app to transfer videos from the Kodak Playful, Model Ze2 to my computer. That's too bad. But anyway, be sure to check the specs before buying so this won't happen to you. I downloaded the program anyway but it wouldn't run. So, I've tried just about everything I know to do and nothing seems to work. An old "FinePixViewer" program keeps popping up every time I try to download a video, but it takes a very long time for it to finally work. I guess technology is trying to force me to buy a newer/faster computer because so many gadgets won't work on poor ole' Bessie anymore despite her having 34 GB left of memory and 4GB of ram.

The camera itself is fun to play with and I like the 1970's film mode, but it would be better if the theme to "Shaft" was being quietly played in the background while using that particular mode. The access doors are very difficult to open and you will probably lose some fingernails until you get it figured out. The Kodak website is not very good.....I never could find a place where I could ask a question directly to technical support. And the web addresses provided in the manual take you to the same web page regardless of the the specifics written into the web address like: [...]. They all take you to the same place and you have to hunt and peck where you want to go and what you're looking for. And they have no Ze2 demos to watch - go figure. And though Windows XP is listed in a drop menu, when I click on it absolutely nothing happens. So much for Windows XP help.

I'm giving it 3 stars because the doors are a pain, and the website is inadequate. But since I don't own a computer that will allow the Kodak program to work I can't fairly judge the quality of the videos. When I can get FinePixView to play them they look alright. I have yet to connect the Kodak Playful directly to my HDTV to see how the HD (720) quality and sound are, and I will do that and report back. I am very interested especially in the sound quality since I'm a musician/music teacher and like to record my students playing.

UPDATE: 2.17.12
I used the Kodak Playful to record my daughter playing guitar in her school's talent show. It did a good job and I was finally able to upload the video to my old computer. Also, I ended up breaking off the door that covers the USB plug which was nearly impossible to open without losing fingernails and then equally impossible to shut close again. The plug stays inside without the door and though I hated doing it, it works much better now.
text_fidelity_b: Kodak PlayFull ZE2 Waterproof Video Camera with 2x Optical Zoom and 2-Inch LCD Screen (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Sony XBR-65A8G 65 Inch TV: BRAVIA OLED 4K Ultra HD Smart TV with HDR and Alexa Compatibility - 2019 Model Overall, I really love this TV. The picture is great. Our last HD TV was good but sometimes it showed all the imperfections. I mean, you could see the makeup on the actors faces. Takes away from the realism. This one has the sharpness without the byproducts? Not sure how to say it.

Setting this up was interesting. It comes in a box that is actually very easy to remove it from. The screen is huge and very thin. I was afraid we were going to break it. It is very light for it's size, basically the same weight as our old 47" LG flatscreen. We ended up putting it on the stand instead of on the wall mount because it would have been difficult to fit due to the alcove only being about 2 inches wider than the screen. It does seem fairly sturdy on the stand. We laid it flat on the cardboard while attaching the stand. The directions tell you to hold it up while screwing it in, but that seemed a little stupid to me without a few people to hold it. You do need to let it hang at the edge of the table or whatever if you are going to do it that way.

Setting it up with my phone didn't work as easily as they made it seem. I ended up inputting the wifi password and going that way instead of taking the settings from my phone after it sat in the checking mode for a while. It also only seems to have 3 HDMI connections which might not be enough, depending on how many "toys" you have. I was kind of surprise there wasn't more. And maybe there was one more than we didn't understand whether it was usable?

We have Directv, so we have to have a separate controller for that. There is an IR attachment that can be set up to allow you to use the TV remote for both, but it was kind of complicated and once the TV was setup it is too big to go back and move it to check for these things. This may be the biggest problem for us with the TV. As you can see in the picture, it is a tight fit. It is also huge. (good for viewing, not good for moving) So once it is set up, that is it. If you don't attach it to the wall (it doesn't come with the wall hanger) you may want to get some kind of tip protection, especially if you have kids. The screen will break if it falls over based on how thin it is, which would be dangerous.

I received this item free in exchange for my honest opinion. Honestly, if I hadn't gotten it free, I would personally not have bought it because I am not that particular about the TV, even if I appreciate the great picture. It's 100% plug-and-play -- zero effort needed to get it operational. It comes NTFS formatted, which is perfect for my needs. The included cable is short but decently sturdy. Other pluses include an operational light that is easy to see but not distracting and a reasonably compact size. Operational speed has been more than acceptable on both USB 2.0 and 3.0 ports. I didn't track the specific transfer rate, but it performed as well if not better than other USB drives I have.

The only notable negative is the case. It's plastic, as expected, but rather flimsy feeling. This is not a drive that will withstand any measure of being knocked around. An SSD drive would be a better choice if durability is the goal.

This suits my needs perfectly as a very affordable, basic, everyday backup drive that will rarely leave the office. 4.5 stars (due to the plastic case which could have been better) but I'll round up to 5 since it does everything else very well at a reasonable price.

Dell Premier Slim Backpack 14 This laptop backpack is suitable for both genders and all ages, but a busy business traveler might appreciate it most of all, because it is fancy enough to bring to a high-class business meeting. The backpack is padded and well made out of matte-black, water-resistant, "pu leather." This is poly-synthetic leather, which mostly looks and feels like real leather, though it is much less durable than real leather and isn't as thick. It certainly is more water resistant than real leather, so that is an advantage, and it also costs less than leather.

There are pockets for organizing various items, and the laptop sleeve is plush lined to protect a laptop from banging. There is also padding on the back side of the pack to cushion your back from sharp edges, which is an excellent comfort-inducing addition to the design. The zipper closure is high quality and should resist snagging and breaking.

All in all, this is a high quality backpack for those who prefer not to carry an old-fashioned briefcase.

text_fidelity_a:
Wall Outlet Extender Surge Protector - 6 Outlet Wall Adapter with 3 USB Charging Ports (1 USB-C, 2 USB A), Multi Plug Outlets Wall Mount with Top Phone Holder for Home, Dorm Essentail, 490 Joules There has been an unpleasant shift, from who is responsible for supplying the power adapters for USB powered appliances. And, for the number of simple household appliances that now require those adapters. I suppose that I can see the logic in it. Newer electrical devices now require lower power. Thence, adapters. At first, they came with the device, like cell phones were supplied with the wall adapters. Eventually, you had to buy your own adapters. Even now, you have to be careful in selecting an adapter. There are basic ones that only have 3 amps. Some have 5 amps or more. Some only split all their power between multiple ports. Some are 'smart' and provide all the amps needed to multiple devices. Now, that's pretty much the rule. You gotta do it yourself and you better know what you're looking for. Disappointment is more common than satisfaction, in this new game.

These outlet adapters from Mifusa probably wouldn't have been my optimum choice, had the listing been a little more informative. But, based on what I read and how it works, it will do well enough.

The six outlets are too close together for bulky plugs or those that have the transformers built into the plugs. The total amperage across all three USB ports is only 3 amps. So, don't look to power multiple USB devices efficiently. Easy to assemble, easy to use. A beginner will get the hang of viewing with a little use with progressively smaller apertures as magnification is increased. There are viewing techniques available on YouTubes to investigate.

text_fidelity_a: Michael Kors Access Gen 4 MKGO Smartwatch- Lightweight Touchscreen Powered with Wear OS by Google with Heart Rate, GPS, NFC, and Smartphone Notifications I have so many feelings about this watch. First off, set up was a breeze. You just open your app store and get the Google app directed. Pairing and synching up your info is very easy. The watch is very beautiful! I was scared the crystals would rub right off like glitter, but I have not had any issues so far. Now for all the bad stuff.. first and foremost the battery life is terrible. I would give it 9-10 hours max. I'm not much of an app person either, so if you are then that means your battery life will be even lower. It has its own charger, so that means you'll have to carry it around with you, especially big your planning to go out after work or school which is very inconvenient. I with it was a standard C USB charger so I can just use my phone charger, but sadly that's not the case. I did an experiment to see how long the battery would last. I charged it to 100%, and left it in my desk right before bed. In the morning at 8 am, I am at 15%. Whoa. Yeah, the battery is just really really terrible. So I thought I'd just change the battery settings..well there is only one other option and that is to go into battery saving mode where all it will display is the time. That in my opinion defeats the purpose of a smart watch. Other than that, I love how I can customize watch faces by using my social media, or pick from a pre made list by Michael Kors. You can also get email notifications, download apps like Google keep to take notes by speaking into your watch, as well as use Google pay, activity tracker, weather, and pause and play music without taking out your phone. So yeah, if your okay with a short battery life, then everything else about this watch is awesome. Just giving you the real tea. Hope you found this review helpful.

text_fidelity_a: SABRENT USB 3.0 Tool Free Enclosure for 2.5” and 3.5” Internal SATA Hard Drives (EC-KSL3) I was all set to return this because it would not recognize my Seagate 4TB SSHD. In disk management it showed up as GPT protective partition. After googling, I found that the only way to get past this was to use Diskpart and Clean the drive--that meant wiping out everything on the drive. Since I had already cloned it, I went ahead and used the Clean command and wiped it out. Still couldn't do anything with the drive in disk management. So using Diskpart again, I used the command, Create Partition Primary. At this point, Diskpart couldn't do anything else. It would not create a volume to format, so I had to use Disk Management to create the volume and format it to exFat. I should state that the drive was recognized by my computer internally when it was connected to a Sata port, but once it was put into the Sabrent, it's drive information was changed and made unusable until I performed the procedure above. Not sure why this happened, maybe because it's a SSHD, but I kinda doubt it since I had no problems with the drive when connected to a Sata Port.
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT USB 3.0 Tool Free Enclosure for 2.5” and 3.5” Internal SATA Hard Drives (EC-KSL3)

text_fidelity_a:
Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer) UPDATE: Local retailer slashed prices and a buddy bought a new +2 (new packaging) and found : new packaging doesn't come with HDMI cable, or the external mic adaptor. He promptly returned it and got an "old packaging" and now had all the equipment. Why the "new packaging" costs more than the "old packaging" is beyond me. The "new packaging" mimics the Roam2 packaging, with no see thru "bubble" at the top of the box - BEWARE!!!

FYI - BB discontinuing the Contour line and the mounts are all 50% off, and the camera(s) are $100 off.

This is a dual review, as I own both the Contour + 2 and the Contour Roam2. I don't work for nor do I have any affiliation with Contour. I've had the Roam2 for more than 6 months, but held off writing this review until I had the +2 to compare it to. Although I don't own a GoPro, several friends do and I do their video editing so I'll chime in on the Contour vs. GoPro at the end.

MOUNTS:
Contour uses the same proprietary mounts across their lineup, so interchangeability between the two should be fairly easy (but doesn't always work out that way). I've found some to be flimsy(hat mount), while others are damn near bomb proof(suction cup)! The rotating lens means you can mount it in just about any position, however it is difficult to know that you've framed the shot with the correct orientation! Had an important video recorded upside down - laser level only lets you know it's level, not if it's upside down! One of the best features I've found is the ¼ by 20 thread on the bottom of the Contour, pretty much universal to all modern cameras and there's a TON of mounts out there reasonably priced.

SOFTWARE:
The Storyteller program needs to be installed on your computer and is fairly easy to use, but not intuitive, you need to play around a bit before you can figure everything out. The editing ability is extremely limited. (I use imovie). Software is free, and although you can use the camera(s) without first updating I suggest you do that first! The +2 also has an app that I use on my iPhone 5 - it too is free and pretty easy to use - but not as capable as the Storyteller program. The downside is you HAVE to use the Storyteller program to change settings on the Roam2, AND you have to use it if you want to use any of the GPS data with the +2.

ROAM2:
Got this for Xmas last year and immediately swapped the included 4GB micro SD for a 16GB. SUPER easy to use - charge, point, and slide the slider to the on position. Video quality is good, first few outings I had it set for 1080@30 and was very happy. In editing I found one clip I had to slow down and was slightly disappointed at the quality - since then I've got it set for 720@60 and haven't had any issues - video quality is still good (even in slow mo). Low light does induce more "noise" to the video, but if there's ambient light (streetlights etc.) you can still get decent vids. Sound quality isn't all that, it's usable, but in high winds or at speed - forget it. Battery life is really good at around 2 hours. The camera itself is very well built, one of my first uses it got throw (by an idiot) about 8ft into about 4 inches of water over concrete - few scratches, but still kept recording. This led me to look for something to help protect the aluminum body - Glock Tape, works amazing, adds some protection, but most importantly gives it some GRIP!

CONTOUR +2:
Only had it for a week or so, really wanted it due to the Bluetooth (to help frame shots) and was wanted the waterproof housing (worried about watersports damage on an upcoming trip) the GPS would be a plus. Once again amazing build quality - this things tough as nails. First thing I did was hook up to Storyteller and get the latest firmware update - less than 5 minutes later I was off and running! Pairing the Bluetooth took a couple of attempts, but once connected has excellent range (20 or so feet with obstructions - close to 50ft line of sight!). Using the app you can check status of battery, GPS, and memory as well as change settings and start stop recording - wish you could watch videos but oh well. The app has about a one second delay between what the camera "sees" and what you see on your phone - pretty amazing! Attached to my suction cup mount and went for a drive - took about 30 seconds for the GPS to lock on the first time (since then it only takes maybe 5 seconds). GPS is accurate. The video quality is great! Uploaded vid into storyteller and the GPS data was also great - until I exported it then there was a lag of about 5 seconds between the data being displayed and the video. Waterproof housing is bulky, yet seems a bit flimsy - still not sure it could survive 200 ft of water. Came with HDMI to hook up to TV - works really well. Haven't used the mic adaptor yet. Battery life seems to be around 1.5 hours, but spare batteries are cheap.

[[ASIN:B007PUC1UU Wasabi Power Battery and Charger Kit for Contour 2350, 2450, 2900, C010410K and ContourHD, ContourGPS, Contour+, Contour+2]]

COMPARISON:
Even though the video specs are the same between the +2 and the Roam2, the video quality of the +2 is noticeably better - even in low light. Sound quality on both suffers in high winds or speed. They both have the proprietary T-rail mounts on both sides, but the ¼ by 20 thread is about an inch further back on the +2. The Roam2 is waterproof without housing to about 3ft, but the +2 has the waterproof housing. The +2 also allows for filming while charging. The +2 has the HDMI out, as well as a jack for external mic. The +2 has the Bluetooth app, plus GPS - that combined with replaceable batteries and the better video make it worth the extra money.

CONTOUR vs. GOPRO:
I absolutely love the form factor and the mounting options available for the Contours. The Contour line has their own proprietary mounts, but the ability to use the ¼ by 20 thread mounts for other cameras (even the GoPro mounts) plus the rotating lens means there's just more ways to mount the Contour. That being said the GoPro Hero3 flat out destroys the video quality of the Roam2, and slightly edges out the +2. Of course this difference (even over the Roam2) is completely removed once video is uploaded to Youtube or other sharing sites as they compress the video during upload! I've yet to see a GoProH3 recording 1080 go for more than 75 minutes. Sound quality between all three is about the same. The GoProH3 app uses wifi - and has about a 3-4 second delay - still works for framing shots, but not much else. The GoPro also has the advantage in that you can change settings in camera - but it is a complicated affair(the +2 only allows you to choose between two predetermined settings). GoProH3 doesn't have GPS, or rotating lense. Contour recently lowered the price on the +2 it's now $50 cheaper than the GoProH3. Also it seems they changed pricing on their mounts - I went with the Contour line because of the simplicity of their system, more mounts, cheaper price, and the form factor. Now that they're cheaper it's a no brainer.
text_fidelity_b: Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT UPDATE: after installing the latest map update and waiting for a very long time for the install software to do its thing and worrying if it had actually finished the install because after about an hour my computer said "the application has unexpectedly quit," the device seems to be working perfectly.

Overall, I like the 2595LMT. It boots and finds the satellites faster and has more information available.

Pros:
1. I can press the lower left "Arrive time" button and change it to a variety of readouts: miles remaining, altitude, time via.
2. Voice command works, mostly, especially on simple commands like "Go Home." More complex commands, like an address, return a wide variety of responses, most of them wrong. (Why it's searching the entire United States when it knows where I am and should be looking locally is beyond me.) I liked the old way of narrowing search to State, then City, then Address. Now it just asks you for the whole address, which it likely doesn't understand.
3. It's slimmer and lighter.
4. Easy to import my favorites from my old Nuvi into the 2595LMT. Using a PC, after plugging the old Nuvi into a computer using the USB port,

a. Navigate until you find the "current.GPX" file on the old Nuvi and
b. Copy it to your desktop (this is also a way to make a backup should you desire.)
c. Rename the file: replace "current" with any word you want, as long as it's not "current") so that it is names "anyword.gpx"
d. Attach the new Nuvi 2595LMT to the computer and navigate until you find the folder with its "current.gpx" file.
e. Copy the "anyword.gpx" file from the desktop into the same folder where the "Current.gpx" file resides.
f. Disconnect and restart. All the old favorites will be added to the current list in your new Nuvi.

5. It doesn't say "recalculating" when you disregard its directions
6. It has lane indicators: a series of arrows in the upper left that tell you which lane to get into to make the next turn. Very cool.
7. Touch screen allows scrolling like a smartphone, at least on some screens.
8. Allows you to add/edit shortcuts like a PC. You can create and move icons around so that you can get to a particular feature with one touch.
9. Micro-SD card only
10. Bigger screen
11. 3-D view of the road
12. Speed limit indicator and simultaneous readout of your actual speed that turns red if you exceed the local speed limit. (I wish it bonged quietly when the speed limit changed to remind you that you have to go slower or can go faster.)

Cons:
1. Sadly, on my unit (even after map and software updates) when I say, "Find Place" it immediately crashes and reboots. And if I say, "Find City" it ignores me, even if I ask it to find New York or Los Angeles. I may try reinstalling the software in case it loaded incompletely for some reason. (UPDATE: I waited a couple of weeks and tried updating the maps again. This time it fully installed and happily all the voice commands now work very well. This alone is a good reason to get is unit. Typing while driving is difficult and dangerous. Voice command is simply wonderful and something I've always wanted in a Garmin.)
2. Stuff has been moved around so that the interface is a bit foreign. For instance, "Favorites" are now "Saved Places" and trying to save or edit a saved place is confusing until you get the hang of it.
3. Doesn't have a powered cradle anymore, only a standard mini-USB on the back. Not a real problem, but it's slower to hook up and remove. I used to be able to drop it on the cradle and go. Now I have to find the end of the cable and thread it into a small port on the back. Minor.
4. The traffic function in my opinion is a joke. Driving LA freeways at most times involves congestion and some delay. It's simply the way it is. The Garmin hates congestion and is constantly trying to get you around it. Thus it's constantly bonging and telling me to get off the freeway to take surface streets, assuming they are magically uncongested when in reality the surface streets during rush hour are ten times worse. I'm pretty much going to ignore its traffic suggestions and may turn it off altogether. If you buy the amazon basics power cord [[ASIN:B003N2POXK AmazonBasics Vehicle Power Cable with Mini-USB Connector for GPS and Other Mini-USB Devices]] it doesn't have a built in traffic receiver and thus defeats the annoying and constant attempts to route you around congestion. Simply put, don't believe the alternate route is going to save you any time. Getting onto surface streets during rush hour is a recipe for even longer delays.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT

Microsoft Arc Touch Mouse (Black) It couldn't be sexier. It couldn't be cooler. The packaging alone is pretty awesome, neat and spare and clean but with a certain wow factor. (It took me a while to figure out that, yes, there actually is a magnet in there that snaps the cover shut!) Compared to my Logitech V450 Nano, the Microsoft Arc Touch definitely wins in the design category. The handling is different, and it will take some getting used to, but I do like the look and feel over other Microsoft mice I have used in the past. The flick-scroll feature will be greatly appreciated by those who have to scroll through a lot of information. The page up/page down points might be handy as well but, again, will take some getting used to.

So those are the pros. The cons, for me, are more of a personal preference-thing. Some will find the click factor as satisfying as a straight-shift sports car. With my arthritis, I prefer the Nano, which is just easier for me to click. What some might find to be a certain yielding mushiness in the Nano, I far prefer to the Microsoft Arc Touch. That's just me. I also like that I have more control over how I define the behavior of my Nano over the Arc Touch; I'm actually quite addicted to my left-scroll "back" and right-scroll "next" designations. DH is going to love his sexy new mouse.

Finally, I had one weird thing happen when I went to the web site listed in the manual for a tutorial: The site looked nothing like anything from Microsoft and appeared to be a redirection of some kind. I didn't dare click on anything on that page. (If this is some partner of Microsoft's, then they should warn users in the documentation.)

text_fidelity_a:
Fire TV Stick with Voice Remote This product has a lot of promise, but fails to deliver in some areas, and is just plan not user friendly in others.
My experience on this product was that it arrived a day late, and when it arrived it would not work with my Visio High Definition Television. The TV either did not recognize it or it did not recognize my TV. So I dragged another High Definition Television into the room that I had (LG) and it immediately began working. Set up was fairly simple, however some of the setup features are where my annoyance began. This device every now and again asks for codes for WiFi and other settings that were already input. Things like Hulu and Netflix ask me every now and again if I want to sign up or login as an existing user. Why does it randomly do this? My Roku remembered me, why cant this. Amazon Prime offers password protection to prevent family members or other unwanted individuals from charging content to your credit card through a six digit pin. However the only way to input that pin (other than downloading an app to your phone) is to use an awkward scroll wheel, and additionally oddly marked buttons to get through the numerous number menu options. It is a bit of a pain. The voice control feature is a waste of money, it only finds items that Amazon can charge you for. I attempted to look up Thomas the Train for my daughter which was not only available free for Prime Members but was also on Netflix and Hulu which I had and was free, instead all it would find was items that Amazon could charge for. This is a common problem with the voice command feature. This when coupled with the horrendous navigation menus and difficulty finding what you want make this a poor choice considering other options from Roku, Apple TV and others. A little more tweaking and this could be a great product.
text_fidelity_b: Fire TV Stick with Voice Remote

Gskyer Telescope 600x90mm AZ Astronomical Refractor Telescope for Kids, Adults Astronomy, German Technology Scope Even though I have always had an interest in astronomy I was never able to work a course in this subject in my college schedule or afterwards. When I saw this telescope offered I realized that now I had both the time and the means to explore my interest a bit further. I had very little difficulty setting the scope up, and spent some time familiarizing myself with the various components. I practiced using this by checking out objects in my neighborhood, and managed to get an 'up close and personal' view of some birds in a neighbor's yard and quickly realized that this scope was powerful.

That evening I took the scope to an upstairs window to see what I could see, and despite the pesky street light was able to get a great view of the full moon (btw did you know that it sparkles a bit?). I saw details that I had only seen in photos before which was fascinating. Then I decided to take a look at Mars, which was near the Moon that evening. That is when things got complicated. The finder scope and the main scope need to be synced, and I don't know how to do this (yet). With some fiddling, and aided by Mars' close proximity to the Moon I was able to find Mars, which was exciting but for some reason it was distorted (it had a starburst appearance). My husband and I fiddled with various lenses and combinations to try to eliminate this but were unsuccessful. The experimentation was further complicated by the touchiness of the stand....it was difficult to make small, smooth adjustments and to keep the scope locked in position. Some of this is no doubt due to our in expertise, some I think is due to the equipment.

My enjoyment of this scope would have been much greater if more instructions had been provided. We discovered, more or less by accident how to lock, at least partially, the scope into place. We managed to make some focusing adjustments by trial and error. Even some rudimentary instructions in a small booklet or even a sheet or two describing how to adjust, focus and lock the scope as well as an illustration of the scope with all the components clearly labeled with a brief description of their function would have been greatly appreciated. This is a basic instrument, one that will primarily be used by beginners or novices who will not necessarily be familiar with this equipment. Basic instructions should have been included. As it is my unfamiliarity with the various aspects of the telescope make following many of the instructions I do find on-line difficult to follow.

Despite this problems I am enjoying my new toy. I found the stand to be steady, and the tray located on the stand to be a handy place to put lenses and covers. As I mentioned earlier this is a surprisingly (at least to this beginning user) powerful scope. I'm going to play around with this some more, and will probably upgrade some of the lenses and add some accessories based on my experiences. Besides star gazing I think this will be a great item to watch birds or wild life, and it is certainly portable and forgiving enough to take on a camping trip.
text_fidelity_b: Gskyer Telescope 600x90mm AZ Astronomical Refractor Telescope for Kids, Adults Astronomy, German Technology Scope

You can just grab it and point and shoot using it while in the "automode" setting, but the resulting pictures may leave you a little disappointed depending upon the photographic conditions. To get the highest quality photos you must become familiar with how this little beauty works. Unfortunately, you might have to print out and tote the manual with you when you find yourself in situations where your pictures aren't what you'd like, or you can't figure out how to do certain things like know what's behind the flashing icon error message, or how to simulate different types of film, or can you choose between clarity, reduced noise and dynamic range? This is not really a simple "point and shoot" camera and all images will turn out great. You will have to study it, practice with it, and most of all have patience and you will be pleasantly rewarded for your efforts. Though the indicators vary with camera settings, there are 23 different indicators just for shooting mode, and 12 for playback mode, not to mention the date/time stamp, battery level, and indicator. It can get confusing.

Although a basic manual booklet is included with the camera, a much more detailed manual must be uploaded from the enclosed CD and then all 125 pages can be printed out or read from your computer monitor. The manual covers all the material in the booklet almost page for page but includes much more information about features the booklet leaves out and the booklet will refer you to specific pages in the manual for more information. Also, in the manual are about 50 FAQ's that are very useful. I am a manual reader, (having written many technical SOP's) and appreciate having well-written and well thought out manuals that are understandable and succinct. Though I would have preferred a manual that I don't have to upload to my computer, it is well-written and many useful pictures are included.

This camera is loaded with many different options/features but accessing and understanding many of them will require reading the manual. For people who don't want to be bothered with all the bells and whistles this camera may be more than they need. I can see very serious photographers using this camera. Reading through the manual I have compiled a list of some of the various modes, options and features available:

Digital Zoom
Movie Mode
Silent Mode
Variable ISO settings
Image size selection
Aspect Ratio selection
Intelligent Face detection
Scene Position
Shooting Modes
EXR Mode
Film simulation
Dynamic Range
White Balance
Continuous Photography
Photometry - multi, spot, average

Playback Options:
Erase
Slide Show
Red-eye Removal
Image Rotation
Protection from accidental deletion
Crop
Resize
Voice Memo
Print Order
Time Difference
Format

Pages 37, 67-68, 86-87, 97-103, and 104-107 would be good to print out and keep with your camera as they contain tables of various camera functions and a trouble shooting chart.

I have taken many pictures and movies inside and out, light and dark, with this camera set on various settings. And though I have practiced with it now for several weeks, I still need to often refer to the manual when I choose to vary from automode. Some things I have found especially desirable are:

Silent Mode - I attend classical music concerts where flash photography is prohibited. This mode will silence all beeps and flashes.

Large viewing screen on the back of the camera. It is exactly 5.5cm x 4.0 cm.

Digital Zoom - extremely good. I attended a local minor-league baseball game and sat far away on the grass well beyond the playing field. I was able to fully zoom and still get good, clear, close-up shots of the players with no blurring.

Movie Mode - Completely surpasses any other I've experienced so far. Images are clear, colorful and the sound quality is excellent. Camera noise was heard and recorded while using the "zoom" function in Movie Mode though it was not very loud.

Multi-frame play back function is very useful to quickly scan for a particular picture.

Fine Pix Viewer Program was very easy to install on my computer. I use Windows XP.

Very good photography in low-light conditions.

Also some things I did not find particularly desirable but are not major flaws:

I cannot directly burn a CD using the Fine Pix Viewer Program which comes with this camera. I have to use another camera program, import the pictures into it and then burn a CD.

Very easy to accidentally turn it on or off and easy to get misfires.

The zoom lever is too sensitive. I have learned with practice to barely move it very slowly.

The camera does not give helpful suggestions on how to get a better picture as does my HP R717.

Not HD capable.

The higher the ISO the grainier the picture though a higher ISO is desirable when shooting in dim/low light levels. I have set the ISO level to 200 and that seems to produce the best pictures so far.

Almost too many options, modes and functions to choose from. Though you can immediately begin to take pictures using Automode, it will take time to fully understand the many other aspects and features this camera has.

In Summary:

I can find no major complaint concerning this camera. It takes excellent clear and colorful photos even in situations where I least expect it - indoors with no flash. Any poor quality pictures I have taken are not the fault of the camera but due to the photographer's ignorance of how to use/understand properly the many features of the camera. The basic mechanics of such things as battery and memory card installation are very easy. Battery charging is a very simple process and battery life seems long. The manual is detailed and covers more than I would probably care to know. This is almost more camera than I need, though I will continue to use it and will update this review as necessary.

UPDATE 2.9.15 - Been using this camera all these years and now it's beginning to show it's age and giving me some problems. The viewing screen on the back has a vertical big black bar but it doesn't appear on the actual pictures. And the lens cover doesn't always completely open when the camera is turned on. I still use it but it might be time to think about a replacement. It's been good though so I really don't have any complaints.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm Finepix F70EXR 10MP Super CCD Digital Camera with 10x Optical Dual Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.7 inch LCD

Construction quality is very solid. There are 8 outlets - 4 for surge only (and are always on); 4 with surge and battery backup. My cable modem (a Motorola) and router (a Linksys) get about 60 minutes of run time off of the battery, which is more than enough for my needs.

Highly recommend for a mid-level UPS system.

text_fidelity_a:
PSB Alpha P5 Bookshelf Speaker - Black Ash I'm not an audiophile, nor do I have fancy audio equipment to measure, compare, etc. I'm just a guy who likes music. So that that as you want. That said, not that I've finally managed to get these hookedup, I can say I"m super pleased.

The look is sleek and compact. The black will fit into any modernist style, not so much if you're more rustic/wood-based decor.

The sound is rich and clear, especially if one doesn't push volume super high. There isn't a deep low bass, but that's to be expected with bookshelf speakers so I don't consider that a flaw. You can perhaps deepen the bass a bit by moving them close to the walls/floor, but I found that muddies the sound for me. Not horribly so, but noticeably. If you're looking for chest-pulsing bass therefore, you'll want to add a sub-woofer. If you don't need that, the bass coverage is fine. Mid-range and high are good as well, without sounding tinny or hard or thin, including at high volume. Vocals are clear and what I"d call natural-sounding or smooth (I recognize those are vague). Vocals stayed true through several genres (rock, singer-songwriter, prog rock, etc). Instruments also were clear. You can pick out individual instruments on ensemble pieces for instance, classical piano comes out warm and clear and stands out within orchestral concertos. Full orchestras sound fine, maybe not as full.

For their price, these are an excellent set, better than certainly most bookshelf speakers I've owned, and I don't think worse than any I've owned. I'd call them significantly better than cheap speakers, and yeah, not as good as 3000 dollar speakers I've heard, but most of us don't have that kind of money for speakers. These are a sweet spot for sound and cost. Highly recommended
text_fidelity_b: PSB Alpha P5 Bookshelf Speaker - Black Ash

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Buds (1st Gen) – Wireless earbuds with immersive sound, active noise reduction, and Alexa I've been using these for a couple of months and find that while I like them, I prefer a competitor's product in terms of sound quality and the ability of the product to stay in my ear. I have tried the different options that come with them to get a better fit and stay in my ear tighter to no avail.

For outdoor activity, I cannot wear these. They fall out of my ear and I lose them. However, indoors I love the Alexa integration. If they could make them in a way they stay in my ear, they would be perfect. Last night, one fell out and went into the garbage disposer. Luckily, it was not on and water wasn't running or it would have been gone.

As they work loose quickly, sound quality and volume diminishes. They do have good bass response when tightly fitted in your ear. If I am sitting still listening to music or an audio book, they work great. As I start to move around, they loosen up and sound poor and are at risk of falling out.

Overall, I do have a use for them. I love the ability to use Alexa. I wish they could do Alexa independent of a mobile device via wi-fi, which they cannot. I love the ability to recharge them from the case when traveling. The case is hard shell and very protective of the earbuds. The case is probably the best part of the product.
text_fidelity_b: Echo Buds (1st Gen) – Wireless earbuds with immersive sound, active noise reduction, and Alexa

On a fairly busy day with the app running in the background on my iPhone the whole time, I was able to wear the watch from 6 a.m. until I went to bed around 10. The other three android watches I've tried didn't make it to dinner.

But this doesn't have a speaker.

Why doesn't this have a speaker?

One of the indispensable features of my Apple watch is being able to answer a call quickly when I have stepped out of the room my phone is in. I have lupus. I can't run. People somehow seem to know to call about something important when I've gone to the bathroom or stepped out to the mailbox. I'm close enough to be connected to my phone, but not close enough to answer it.

This never happens with spam calls. Just the ones from the people I won't be able to get back to through their nightmare phone menus.

The lack of this feature makes the watch unsuitable for me, and that makes me sad, because the iPhone is a begware spamming disappointment machine these days, and I really want to move to android.

Wavlink Dual Bay External Hard Drive Docking Station, USB 3.0 to SATA I/II/III for 2.5 or 3.5in HDD, SSD with Fixed Bezel, Support Offline Clone Function, UASP 6Gbps [ 2x16TB Support] Seems to do what it is supposed to do. I tried it out on 2 new drives that I needed to setup for a new computer. I didn't test the clone function. My computers all have m.2 drives for the OS, and that is the only drive I would clone. This is not set up for an m.2 drive.

That said, the tab things are hard to get it, but are solid once they click in. I also found it difficult to get the drives to click in, especially the second one, once the first was in. Also, you cannot hot swap the drives. You have to eject the docking station, change the drives and reattach the docking station to change or add a drive on your computer. Cloning may be different, if you are doing it offline

Once in, Windows 10 had no problems recognizing the drives and working with them. If you keep internal drives for backing up, this is an easier way to use the drives and then put them in storage. The dock can stay by the computer. Turn it on when you need it, and turn it off when ejecting drives. Overall, so far it works really well and I love the shiny red cover. Brightens up the boring office full of grey.

text_fidelity_a:
for New Solis Lite Listing, go to: https://www.Amazon.com/dp/B08YKB6VMN?ref=myi_Title_dp I love this thing! I only returned it because I didn’t get it in time for my travel and searched high and low for any local stores to sell them and I found 1! Prices were pretty much the same everywhere online.

I went through my carrier, Verizon and sure you can get a jet pack or some mobile WiFi device but you still have to pay monthly charges (like a mobile phone) which isn’t worth it for me. I don’t travel often so I don’t want to pay for something I won’t be using.

This device is awesome! You don’t need a SIM card which seemed like a requirement for other mobile WiFi devices during my search. They have many plans you can choose from or pay as you go. It’s wireless and charged fully quickly. You can track your usage and purchase more data (if you’re not on an unlimited plan). Once you’ve used up data, you’re cut off so there’s no surprise overage costs.

The app for me wasn’t as user friendly but support was available right away via app. I they believed there was a glitch with mine. The remaining data kept changing (significantly) at first. After resetting it, seemed to fix the problem.

I didn’t see an option to have users enter password every time. My kids set their devices to auto connect so they would connect without knowing (if I didn’t check usage). This drained my data. The other negative thing I would say is that it tells you how many devices are connected but not who or what is connected unless I just didn’t see the option (again, not user friendly to me). All this is minor given my research on what was available.

Why didn’t I use my Verizon hot spot? I wanted to make sure I was able to connect without issues and upload/download without issues. My experiences with the 4g hot spot was terrible. The 5G isn’t as bad (but I didn’t know that since I had just upgraded my phone).
text_fidelity_b: for New Solis Lite Listing, go to: https://www.Amazon.com/dp/B08YKB6VMN?ref=myi_Title_dp

text_fidelity_a:
Sony FDRAX53/B 4K HD Video Recording Camcorder (Black) An astonishing example of technology like nothing I've ever seen before.

It's been forty years (!) since I first saw a video camera in high school, a big b/w camera with a backpack that contained the batteries and internals. It was impressive! Then we used a kind of mini-VHS video recorder to share kid videos with our parents maybe 15-20 years ago. Then I got an iPhone which had kind-of video capabilities. So I guess I was ripe to be blown away by this Sony FRAX53/B.

It's small and compact, like a small football. The swing-out screen is breathtakingly crisp and the internal operating system and menus are not only in color, but accompanied by clear, bright sound! I charged the battery and took a video of one of my cats. I could not believe the clarity of the image when I viewed it on the screen! The video is of such high quality that it's easy to overlook the still camera, which is remarkable. High-resolution, bright images. The "Photo" button is kind of oddly placed, it's not easy to operate it while you're holding the device with its right-side hand strap. You can also use a "Manual" mode and twist the lens to achieve custom focus. There's a 20X optical magnification which ought to satisfy anyone.

The Sony software is thorough and functional. The camcorder will transfer photos and video wirelessly if you have a fairly modern computer. I had to use a PC laptop rather than my elderly Mac. That meant using Windows 10, which led to some baffling moments trying to figure out if anything was working.

Between the Sony software and the camcorder and our WiFi setup and Windows 10 I found that the best thing to do sometimes was just WAIT. Windows would give me bad information and I would misinterpret that as an error. Ignore what Windows is telling you and be patient while the FDRAX53/B does its work.

The printed manual is basic and you'll want to spend time reviewing the online documentation. I'm still trying to figure out how to use the Sony FDRAX53/B and a "U-Stream" service to get a live stream going. There is a LOT of technology packed into this camcorder! Expect to spend some time reviewing it all. As I mentioned, Sony packed a TON of features in this device, and there's a learning curve to really understand and appreciate them all.

If you're planning a vacation or expecting a newborn child, BUY THIS CAMCORDER! You cannot take enough videos and photos of your kids when they're young, and the same goes for vacations -- this camcorder is small enough to tote with you (it does not like fog or water, though!) and the QUALITY of the images are incredible! It's not so heavy that it's going to be a burden.

The sound is very good, and there's a "gun" style microphone if you want to A) avoid wind noise B) capture audio of what you're shooting (like at a kid's soccer game) rather than local chitchat.

One thing that occurred to me while I was fiddling with the camcorder in my right hand, that being that if you were holding one of your kids in your left hand and the camcorder in your right hand and they both began to slip... which would you grab? This camcorder is THAT nice. Between the quality of the camcorder and its fantastic lens and the Sony software for image management and manipulation, this could be a major hobby in and of itself. You can easily edit, trim and combine videos with sound and add captions and text. For a consumer level product, the video and image editing suite is quite impressive. You will want a fairly modern computer, as I mentioned.

Something I come back to again and again as I figure the FDRAX53/B out is the absolute wonder of it. The small size, the quality of images, the ease of operation -- I just can't get over it. Beyond sensational and well into the realm of magical. I've never seen anything like the FDRAX53/B before.
text_fidelity_b: Sony FDRAX53/B 4K HD Video Recording Camcorder (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Keyboard for Business (5KV-00001 ) I bought one of these 9 years ago and got a lot of use out of it. Yeah, the letters all wore off very quickly but I know where the keys are so no big deal. But it was finally time for a new one. The material on the palm rest was wearing out, etc.

I unpacked it and noticed it feels cheaper, oh well, not the first manufacture to make a product from cheaper materials as time goes on...

But the strangest thing... the little nubs you use to position your fingers are on the wrong keys??? On the left hand, it's under your index finger on the F key as expected. But on the right hand, it's under my middle finger on the K key. Makes no sense to have them be under different fingers. The middle finger, index finger I don't care but make it the same on both sides.

I already threw my old one out, and I could get it out of the trash but I tossed the dongle in the trash too would never be able to find it again...

The keys feel is Ok I'm not that fussy about key feel click, etc. but be warned that the communication on this keyboard with the dongle is terrible. It was bad on my original one and it's bad on this one. I was hoping there would be an improvement on that in the 9 years that I had the original.

In the end, unless there is something you really like about this keyboard (for me it was an ergo keyboard with no number pad) I would consider something else.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Keyboard for Business (5KV-00001 )

text_fidelity_a:
Magellan RoadMate 1470 4.7-Inch Widescreen Portable GPS Navigator I've been a Magellan user for several years - have owned four of their GPS systems, and always appreciate how they have improved their products. This unit is my 5th, and replaces a Magellan 4040. After using it for a while I've confident in saying this is the best one yet!

The most visible change is the actual size of the unit. The screen size has been increased, but the unit is thinner and lighter. Very sleek appearance, and the screen is a real joy -- sharp, clear graphics even in the sun, and bigger on-screen buttons for easy use. The mounting system has also been streamlined, and looks and works well. It mounts very easily on a NavMat holder (basically a bean-bag system that I got on Amazon. I'm a huge Navmat fan - makes it a snap to hide the GPS with narry a trace. Best accessory by far for any GPS).

The power connector was not well thought out, however. You have to connect it to the GPS unit AFTER you mount it in the holder. They should have moved the connector it a wee bit to the side to avoid that.

The only button is a slide-type power button on the top. Boot-up time is OK -- not speedy, but not a huge delay either. It does not have a "sleep" mode, so you have to do a cold boot every time. Not a problem in real world use - by the time you get situated in your car, the unit is ready to go.

Voice is clear and easy to understand. Not as natural sounding as a TomTom, but understandable.

Pretty much any recent GPS unit will get you where you want to go. I've found the routing on the Magellans to be very similar to Garmins - could be because they both use the same mapping set (Navteq). The Magellan shines, however, in features that I find helpful. The direction of the next turn is always visible regardless of how far away the next turn will be. Up until recently, Garmin did not offer this (they do now on some of their units). Sounds like a small issue, but I find it very helpful. The Magellan also allows you to very easily exclude a route (or portion). That's a fairly standard feature nowadays, but Magellan allows you to do it in a snap.

In terms of routing, Magellan offers four options (fastest, shortest, most use of freeways and least use). You can see all four options on the map (as a summary) at the same time so you can pick the best one for your needs. Perfect!!

Love the AAA Guidebook, which is a unique Magellan feature. Lets you get details about restaurants and other points of interest just like the paper version from AAA. I used it a lot in my 4040, especially when traveling out of town.

Other unique Magellan features I appreciate is the "ding dong" sound right before a turn (incredibly accurate!) and the fact that the software reminds you to "stay on the current road" when you encounter major exits. Some find that to be nagging, but it has saved me from inadvertently exiting on more than one occasion.

A new feature for Magellan is the lane guidance. Very nicely done. I've used this feature on Navigon units, and found it rather unhelpful. Magellan's implementation is far more useful, with better, clearer graphics. However, lane guidance is not available for every road.

The software is also nicely done - very logical to use. If you're a past Magellan user you can pick this up and use it in a second. If not, there's a short printed user's guide in the box (plus a CD-ROM with more in-depth info) that gets you up to speed quickly. The box also includes the mount, power connector for the car, and a USB cable. It does not include an AC adapter.

OK, now for the bad news. When it comes to customer service, Magellan has been horrid. We're talking so bad it's almost funny. I'm hoping this situation will change - the company was bought by Mitac late last year, and perhaps this will signal a change for the better in terms of customer support. Lord knows, they couldn't get any worse.

The leader, in my opinion, for customer support is Garmin. They are nice to deal with on the phone, answer emails promptly, and offer regular firmware updates. Whenever I buy a GPS as a gift I always buy Garmin since I don't want to saddle the recipient with the miserable service that Magellan offers. It's a shame, since Magellan offers some real benefits over Garmin, and more value for the money. Tom Tom is also decent when it comes to support, but they use TeleAtlas maps which are less complete than NavTeq (sp?).

Bottom line -- if you're looking for a straightforward GPS at a good price, this should be on your short list. It lacks features such as Bluetooth and an MP3 player, but for me, I want a GPS to offer guidance and not entertainment. This has a very robust feature set, great screen, and well-designed software. It also has traffic capabilities -- did not test that feature out, so I can't comment on it.

The "safe" bet continues to be Garmin. You'll pay a bit more, and get less features, but you can be assured of solid support. Whether Magellan's new owners will put them back on the right track (if you'll excuse the horrid, but unavoidable pun) in terms of customer service is not yet clear. I hope so -- they make a great product!

UPDATE: 5/21/09 There's a firmware update on the Magellan site. No new functionality (in terms of new features) but, according to the release notes it improves overall performance. Easy to install - just follow the included step-by-step instructions. It seems like it makes the unit a bit faster, but that could just be my imagination.
text_fidelity_b: Magellan RoadMate 1470 4.7-Inch Widescreen Portable GPS Navigator

Amazon Basics DSLR Camera Backpack (High Density Water-Resistant 840D Polyester) - Ash Gray I just received my new camera backpack today. My initial reaction is amazement. The bag really looks sharp and it is far better-made than I expected it would be.

I shoot professionally and have for decades. My landscape camera is packed in a huge Tarion pack. I love it. This Amazon Basics pack is very nicely designed. I like the fact that the main cargo section unzips on the side that is against your back when you wear it. It lessens the chance of having something fall out on the trail... I've known other photographers who left a zipper open by accident and had a lens fall on rocky terrain.

I wish it had a nice set of built-in battery compartments like the Tarion packs do. Those are really great. I do love the flat bottom on this pack. The Tarion bag doesn't have that feature.

In addition to the durable outer shell and nicely designed cargo area, the Amazon Basics camera backpack also has one of the nicest shoulder strap and waist belt setups I've ever seen. This thing is comfortable to wear. It also has a rain fly to protect my precious cargo.

My landscape gear is in the other pack. This one is for my wildlife gear.

One last thing, I have more room for lenses are other essentials. I guess I need to do more shopping. :o)

Acme Made Skinny Sleeve Medium (Stretchshell Neoprene) Sapphire/Grey AM10341 So... based on the product description, one can assume that any laptop that runs about 13"-14" should fit neatly into this sleeve. Well, not so much, really. When it arrives you'll see that the tag clearly states that it is for the Macbook Pro/Air 13. Nothing else. No Inspirons, no Yogas, and really not my Alienware 13. Oh, I can squeeze it into the sleeve if I work at it, and if I take the plastic insert out, but it's a lot like trying to fit into your skinny jeans after a weekend of Netflix and ice cream. You can do it, but it's not going to be pretty. And unfortunately getting my laptop back out of the sleeve was even harder. I checked the seams after two insertions and removals, and while they look fine now, I fear that repeated use might be hard on them.

So does it protect my laptop? Well, yes and no. It's in there pretty tightly, so the protective layer is stretched thin. And the end sticks out. I simply can't get it all the way into the sleeve. There's maybe a quarter to half an inch that protrudes. Now if I was tossing this into a briefcase or backpack, I wouldn't worry, but as it is, it's still vulnerable to being dropped along that edge or to being rained on or spilled on.

So overall what I would tell you is this: If you don't have a Macbook Pro/Air 13, then compare the measurements of your laptop to those of that model. If you're not close, look elsewhere.

text_fidelity_a:
LG Cinema Screen 55LM8600 55-Inch Cinema 3D 1080p 240Hz Dual Core LED-LCD HDTV with Smart TV and Six Pairs of 3D Glasses (2012 Model) The picture is astounding. A few friends and I watched [[ASIN:B004K4N64E Tron: Legacy / Tron: The Original Classic (Five-Disc Combo: Blu-ray 3D / Blu-ray / DVD / Digital Copy)]] on this, and althought I love the movie, I couldn't pay attention to the movie the first time through. I was too busy staring in awe at the way the clouds in the distant background moved, or the beauty of the image. I was told passive 3D is an image quality drop from HD because it projects half the image to each eye, but I'm calling that theory out. This picture is glorious.

When it upscales images to 3D it can get a little odd. I watched Naruto on it, and some moments were astounding, and some were just odd, as Naruto's eyes seemed to deepen into layers. Overall, I like the upscale. It's an approximation of 3D, but it's a darn good approximation.

My boyfriend wears huge glasses and these fit over them perfectly. On a lark, I put them on over my largest sunglasses, and they still fit, so if you wear glasses, even very large glasses, and you have any concerns that they won't work well with these, stop worrying.

As to connectors, there is one input for composite in, but it comes with a three-into-one adapter for that. The same for component in. Those are the only cable that come with it, so you will need those. I suggest [[ASIN:B003L1ZYYW AmazonBasics High-Speed HDMI Cable (9.8 Feet/3.0 Meters) - Supports Ethernet, 3D, and Audio Return [Newest Standard]]] as they are reliable and implement 3D transmission well. There are four specifications for HDMI, 1.4 being the latest, and not every device or cable fully implements the specification. The signal will downgrade to the lowest component, and with a TV like this, you don't want that component to be your cable. The difference is substantial.

There are four HDMI ports, and it doesn't seem to like connecting to an HDMI switcher. If you have a lot of devices plugged in, and you often find yourself wondering which input the DVD player is using, you'll love this. First, if a device isn't actively sending a signal, it displays as greyed out, and moves to the back of the list. Second, you can name your inputs. You select them from a list (I would have likes to call one Playstation 2, but had to opt for "Game") but it helps a lot.

The remote is kind of like a Wii controller. You wave it around and it points at things on the screen you can select. Very cute. If you find it hard to use, back up a few steps. It's counterintuitive, but it works. The cursor slows down.

For streaming it has the standard YouTube, Netflix and Hulu among others. The only tiny downside is that it doesn't yet support Amazon on demand videos. Plug in a [[ASIN:B005CLPP84 Roku 2 XS 1080p Streaming Player]] and you're set for streaming entertainment. I am in the process of replacing my router. It's in such bad shape that my Pingtest results range from B- to C when connected wirelessly. Whatever caching the set top does, it can provide perfect clarity even in such adverse conditions. Good to know if your Internet can have "off moments".

The energy star note that came on the TV (the yellow tag required by law that you see on all appliances these days) claims that this TV will have an Estimated Yearly Energy Cost of $14 with a range for similar models (45" - 49" TVs) going from $18 to $51. This is "Based on 11 cents per kWh and 5 hours use per day."

I wish I could give this 50 stars. It's perfect.
text_fidelity_b: LG Cinema Screen 55LM8600 55-Inch Cinema 3D 1080p 240Hz Dual Core LED-LCD HDTV with Smart TV and Six Pairs of 3D Glasses (2012 Model)

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I've had this Nuvi 360 since Dec, 2006. It really works well. I carried it with me to DC. Even on foot it was terrific. It knew where all the restaurants and points of interest were and faithfully navigated us around the ancient horse paths of the Virginia/DC area. Believe me, when you pop out of an underground Metro station in the middle of the night and have no idea where you are or which direction to head off in, the ol' Garmin was there.

It's so small it easily fits in a pocket. The built-in battery lasts reasonably long. In the car, the 12-Volt adapter allows the unit to stay on indefinitely. You can select which accent and which gender you want the voice prompts to speak. Australian "Bruce," American "Jill" and a host of other combinations. All very fun. The voice prompts are the best. You really don't need to look at the thing while driving because it's uncanny in telling you what to do when you need to do it. It is amazingly accurate: something like 20 feet. It takes you right to the destination driveway.

It acquires the sats quickly and doesn't get flustered if you violate its recommendation and go in a different route. It just says, "recalculating" and finds another route for you. None of this "make a U-turn, bonehead!" It gives you enough time to make the turns, too. Also, it displays how far it is until the next turn. Very nice. No need to worry if you've missed it.

If you are planning on going to Europe, buy the unit that comes preloaded with both US and Europe maps as purchasing the Europe maps after the fact will really jump the cost unnecessarily.

I haven't used the Bluetooth capability yet but might later...after I get a Bluetooth phone.

The display is quite viewable in daylight and very bright at night, though it can be set to auto-dim at sundown so it's not too bright at night. You can touch the screen and scroll the map under your finger much like Google Maps can, to preview your route if desired. It shows coordinates and you can save them as destinations if desired, even if the location doesn't have an official street address. It is an MP3 player and can display photos and play Audible books on tape. When you are using the MP3 or Audible features, it pauses the file playing back to announce directions, then returns to the file without losing any of the MP3 file or book info. Very nice.

At extra cost, it has the ability to add foreign language dictionaries which can verbally speak phrases and words to you. You can also add Travel Guides and other software via the SD chip slot.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this device. It's accurate, fast, functional and small.

The one thing that doesn't work is the windshield suction mount. It broke before I even used it once. The plastic loops on the suction cup that receive the ball arm's hinge pin are too thin and fragile and broke with just a little normal hinge adjustment.

I recommend the model 010-10908-00 friction mount that looks like a bean bag with a ball arm sticking up. I made something similar by taking an unneeded 1/4" thick mousepad and epoxying a couple of small 1" x 1" angle brackets to the pad to hold the ball arm that I salvaged from the broken suction cup mount.

A friction mount is interchangeable with multiple vehicles, doesn't slide around on the dash and allows complete and rapid removal and/or hiding to avoid theft. Plus, you don't have to glue a disk to the dash for the suction cup to attach to.

UPDATE 10-22-07:
The 360 works well enough; better than most. It should: Five point three bills should deliver one heck of a map!

I've had it since Dec 2006...less than one year. Today I get an offer from Garmin to update my North American map software for a mere point seven bills. That's AFTER the five point three bills I already sunk into this little electronic gizmo.

I heard Garmin has a one year free map update policy, but their website won't let me do it. Not cool. The cost of the unit has already fallen significantly from what I originally paid and now they want more to get it current, within a year of purchase. Not cool at all. Also, impossible to contact by email. Garmin website is in a permanent loop back to itself when clicking on the "contact by email" option. Otherwise, it's call and wait on hold between certain times. Not cool again.

Then a friend says how well his Verizon GPS works on his wireless phone. I look into that. Verizon offers a full time GPS cost and a single use option for under three bucks per use.

For what I have wasted on this Garmin--over five bills and counting upward forever with their unfriendly updates--that's a whole heck of a lot of one-time Verizon uses with what will be the most updated, most accurate database. After all, no one's going to beat the phone company with accurate phone numbers and addresses.

If I hadn't already bought into the Garmin ripoff, I'd definitely go with Verizon's phone based GPS: the phone will always be with you when you need it instead of in the glove compartment in the other car.

And it most likely won't get stolen. It's a darned pain to have to put the Garmin away after each use so some cretin won't bash in a window to steal a very, very expensive toy that could just as easily fit inside a phone.

Go with the phone.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st) The new Kindle arrived within 2 days of my order. I sat down and played around with it for a few minutes and learned the icons but that's all that can be done until it is registered with Amazon. I took it to Toyota while getting my car serviced. Our local Toyota dealer has free WiFi for customers. The Kindle found the hot spot and Amazon recognized the Kindle right away.  It took a few taps around the screen to get started but was easy with a little exploring. Within the time to get an oil change, I had downloaded my ebooks from Cloud and even bought a nice app on sale.  Next I stopped by BestBuy and added a Kindle micro USB to USB cable.  The cable can be used to download ebooks from your PC when not connected to wireless.  Using free Calibre to manage the free ebooks from the Internet, enables covers and metadata for those ebooks that have none.  Calibre will also download the books to Kindle from a PC.  The Fire is great but took some thinking and patience to get it to do all the things I imagined it would do. For instance, ebooks without covers will all look alike and have no title.  This is why it is important to use Calibre for ebook management. Reading ebooks is so much better than it was 10 years ago and this is only the beginning.  The download speed is great.  The reading speed is also great.The storage space is really more than enough.  The 8 Gigabytes of memory is close to 2 warehouses of data.  I read that somewhere on Wikipedia in the middle of the night.  To put it in proportion, imagine having up to 6000 books in your home. The Kindle does not get hot like a netbook and is smaller and lighter too.  The battery life is much better than my 7" netbook also.  Like other customers, I would have liked the micro USB to USB cable included in the box.  3G would be great too.  The best thing about Kindle Fire is the color.  The color is as beautiful as everyone says it is.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st)

text_fidelity_a:
AMD FX 4100 4-Core Processor, 3.6 4 Socket AM3+ FD4100WMGUSBX My old computer was exactly that: Old! It needed some serious work. I was running an Athlon X2 6000+ and an EVGA 9800GT. It was a great system back in the day! But, time took its toll. I was kicking around the idea of getting an Intel i3, since they seem to edge out this chip, and are competitively priced (I never overclock my equipment, so it's at stock settings.) But the future upgradability seemed like it'd be very costly. Over all, this chip performs just fine. I mainly upgraded so I could play Diablo 3, and with an EVGA 550 Ti, I play it on high settings, and it looks as good as I could want it to look. My old machine did just fine with standard productivity stuff, but I wanted to play games that were more recent than WoW. I'm able to do everything I want, with no signs of a lag. If I need to upgrade, I'm banking that the next generation of this chip will see some improvements (though the improvement I'm seeing from my last CPU is leaps-and bounds!) The AM3+ socket will be around for a while. Over all, this is a great chip, and easy on the wallet.

**Update 9/6/12**
I recently purchased Guild Wars 2. The game is fairly CPU-intensive, but the FX-4100 keeps up just fine! I think I'm sitting at around 50% plus load at any given time during actual game play on all four cores. I haven't had a single hiccup or spot of lag yet!

Starcraft 2 is another CPU-heavy application, and coupled with the 550 Ti card, I'm running it on Extreme at 1400x900 resolution, and it's flawless. Again, all four cores are loaded, and quite frequently, they're over 60%. Things get a little warm (35C or so) when compared to when I run other applications. Nothing to worry about!

I have also paid quite a bit of attention to how it runs with Diablo 3. It only uses 2 cores at about 50% load at any given time. That game is more GPU-intensive. I am still very happy with my purchase!
text_fidelity_b: AMD FX 4100 4-Core Processor, 3.6 4 Socket AM3+  FD4100WMGUSBX

I have had it up for a few days and haven't experienced major problems with it. We will see if it stands up to the test of time and gives me 3-4 years of service like my Cisco Linksys devices that are still working 4 1/2 years later.

Nerd Alert - I am a nerd at heart and utilize geek speak way too often. I try to remember that the Amazon audience contains friends, family, and strangers that may or may not know IT.

PROS:
* Feature Rich -
The ZyXEL is 1/2 the price of the comparable Cisco device but it has a much more feature rich set of wireless capabilities. It supports WPS, allowing for easy setup. It supports WDS, allowing you to configure a network that allows you to carry your laptop from room to room in a large house without sacrificing much speed if setup correctly. It can access as a repeater if needed.

* Cabling -
The ZyXEL includes the power supply and a network cable (CAT-5). It supports a standard called MDI/MDIX, which means that you won't need a crossover cable if you connect it to a switch.
* Wireless Distribution Service -
You can make this part of your existing network using WDS, or Wireless Distribution Service, or simply configure it as an access point. I just removed two old Linksys routers from being WDS nodes since replacing my old Actiontec 802.11a/b/g with an Actiontec 802.11b/g/n wireless router. Eventually I will get around to using the ONI port and setting up a network with DD-WRT

CONS:
* LAN ports on the back are are 10/100 -
While the router notes that it supports connection speeds up to 300MbPS it only has two (2) 10MbPS/100MbPS RJ-45 (LAN) connections. Technically you may never truly realize the full throughput available with this device. This is not unlike other wireless access points, such as the Cisco WET610N (single 10/100) or the Cisco WES610N (quad port 10/100 for $10 more). I did what any good geek would do; used it as an excuse to purchase an 8-port Netgear 10/100/1000 switch to replace my 5-port 10/100 switch in my office/lab with the computers and Hyper-V lab systems. I am going to use the Cisco product downstairs with my home server and VMWare ESXi box.

* Setup may be difficult for the average home user -
I most certainly RTFM'd and reading the manual helped. It did take a quick configuration of my network card in order to even get to the point I could setup the device.
The Cisco devices use an APIPA address, which makes setup easier. Why? APIPA is that 169.254.#.# address that your computer gets when it connects to a network that doesn't give out addresses. This allows you to easily setup the Cisco WES610N.
text_fidelity_b: ZyXEL 300 Mbps Wireless N Access Point, Ethernet Client, Universal Repeater, and Range Extender (WAP3205)
